source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Radiation problem paradigm: subjects study a military story (fortress, converging small forces) as a 'story recall' task, then get Duncker's tumour problem with no hint. Only about 30% produce the convergence solution. With a plain hint to use the story, about 75% do. Without any story only about 10% solve it. So the story was stored and usable, but not noticed.
numbers: Standard figures across Gick & Holyoak experiments: ~10% no-analog baseline (several replications), ~30% with story and no hint, ~75% total after hint. Gick & Holyoak 1983 text says only 'a third or less' of those who could use the analogy noticed it. Exp 2 N=88 (3 conditions); Exp 4 N=98.
limits: The 1980 original paper was not opened; these numbers come from the 1983 paper and the 1993 paper that restate them. Hint was non-specific. Some of the ~20-30% may be demand effects (subjects guess the two parts are linked). The military story is structurally imperfect for the tumour problem (Keane's replication got similar results).
agent_relevance: Cleanest proof that the failure is in ACCESS not storage or mapping: the same material works after a nudge. For the agent: a retrieved or stored solved subgoal is useless unless something cues it. A cue at an impasse (S6) is cheap and, under G1, fires only on a failure signal, so it is consistent.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Two analogs are better than one. When subjects read two analogous stories and wrote down how they were similar, they often built an abstract convergence schema as a by-product, and the quality of that schema predicted transfer.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=98: 28 two-similar, 23 two-dissimilar, 47 one-analog+control): no-hint solutions 45% (two analogs, pooled) vs 21% (one analog), G2(1)=6.35, p<.01; total with hint 80% vs 53%, G2(1)=8.36, p<.003. Similar vs dissimilar pair: 39% vs 52% no-hint, not significant. Schema quality (two-analog groups): intermediate schema 40% no-hint / 90% total; poor schema 30% no-hint / 70% total; 90% of those who never solved had written a poor schema.
limits: Schema quality is correlational inside Exp 4 (good problem solvers may write good schemas AND transfer). Later experiments (5, 6) give a causal push. Single-analog baseline here (21% / 53%) was lower than the usual 30% / 75%.
agent_relevance: Direct design hint: do not store one solved case; compare two solved cases and keep the abstracted rule. This is the basis for our 'compare two solved subgoals, store the schema' idea in the subgoal library.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Telling the principle outright or showing diagrams does NOT help from one analog, but helps a lot when paired with two analogs. A verbal statement of the principle with two stories lifts noticing.
numbers: Exp 2 (one analog, N=88): analog+principle about 30% no-hint, same as analog alone (~30%); total G2(2)=2.05, p=.36. Exp 5 (two analogs): with principle 62% no-hint vs 40% without, G2(1)=6.75, p<.01; total 82% vs 67%, G2(1)=4.34, p<.05. Exp 6: diagrams gave 57% vs 37% initial solutions; one earlier dissimilar-pair run with diagrams reached 68% no-hint, 95% total (N=37). Exp 1 (cord problem): analog conditions 71% vs 20% before hint, 98% vs 30% total (G2(1)=15.8 and 30.1); summarising the story did no better than recall.
limits: Instruction effects depend on having two examples to align; one example gives the learner no principled way to find the essential causal part (authors call the failure on one case 'appropriate conservatism').
agent_relevance: Stating a rule in the prompt is weak by itself. The rule becomes usable when it is induced from a comparison. Design the library entry as (two solved cases, aligned, plus the induced rule), not (rule text).

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Authors' account of why a few people still notice a single analog: prior knowledge, demand characteristics, and chance encoding of the story in abstract terms. Noticing depends on semantic retrieval cues in the story.
numbers: About 20% of subjects solved by using the military story with no hint, consistent across experiments. One subject in Gick & Holyoak (1980) mapped it onto a known laser-lightbulb convergence problem.
limits: Discussion is interpretation, not a tested result. Gick & Holyoak 1980 is the source for the lightbulb case and control groups; not opened.
agent_relevance: Retrieval success depends on how the stored item was encoded (abstractly or concretely). When we store a solved subgoal, we should store an abstract restatement next to the concrete one, so both can be matched.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: The core dissociation. Same pairs of stories (Karla the hawk set, 18 to 20 story sets) were used in two tasks. When people RATE how sound an inference from one story to the other would be, they use relational structure. When they are REMINDED of an earlier story by a cue, surface (object) similarity dominates. So retrievability and soundness are governed by different kinds of similarity.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=30, MIT students, 18 sets): soundness analogy M=4.40 vs surface-match 2.80 vs first-order-relations-only 2.74 (F(2,58)=70.51, p<.0001). Reminding: proportion recalled surface-match .78, analogy .44, first-order-only .25 (F(2,58)=75.45, p<.0001).
quote: subjective soundness was highly related to the degree of common relational structure, while retrievability was chiefly related to the degree of surface similarity.
limits: Stories were 2-3 paragraph prose, read then cued after a delay (one week in later experiments). Exp 1 shows a much higher analogy recall (.44) than later experiments (.07 to .12), so absolute analogical access varies by materials and scoring.
agent_relevance: Our retrieval step must not use the same similarity for 'find' and 'trust'. Cheap surface-weighted find, structure-weighted check in code. This is the empirical basis for a two-stage design.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Exp 2 added a literal-similarity (LS) cue (objects + relations + higher-order structure) and gave a 2x2 design. Cues that share objects (LS and surface) are recalled about equally and far better than cues that share only relations (analogy, first-order). Adding higher-order relational structure gave no significant recall advantage.
numbers: Exp 2 (20 story sets + 12 fillers, test one week after study, soundness and similarity rated by separate groups): proportion recalled LS .56, surface-match (SS) .53, analogy (AN) .12, first-order-only (FOR) .09. Soundness: LS 4.41, AN 4.16, SS 2.70, FOR 2.58. Correlation of soundness with recall r(78)=.008, not significant.
limits: Quality-of-reminding score did show an LS/AN advantage but the authors say that measure overestimates relational memory (recall written as a template of the cue). Keyword and proportion measures do not.
agent_relevance: A relational-only match (the thing we want from an analogy) is retrieved about one time in eight by people. An LLM with an embedding retriever may behave similarly: expect surface-near cases to win unless structure is made explicit.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Exp 3 separates object-only matches (OA) from relation matches. Even object-only commonalities, with no shared relations, are recalled more often than pure analogies. But surface plus first-order relations (SS) is recalled much more than objects alone, so access is not just object overlap.
numbers: Exp 3: literal similarity .62 recalled; SS (objects + first-order relations) 52%; object-only (OO) 17%; analogy (relations only, incl. higher order) 7%. Soundness order AN (3.85) > SS > OO (2.38).
limits: Authors note analogy cue stories lacked object descriptions, so the contrast is between sparse and rich cues; natural analogies often differ more than these constructed ones.
agent_relevance: Object overlap and relation overlap both feed retrieval, but only the combination wins. A cue that has the same relations in the same domain words is easiest to match; abstracting away domain words (rewriting the problem in neutral terms) can remove the surface bias and also the surface help.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Exp 4 rules out the 'they never encoded the structure' explanation. After one week, subjects given a forced choice recognition test between an LS and a SS cue chose LS well above chance, so the relational structure was stored. But when asked to choose between an analogy cue and a first-order-only cue, they were near chance. So the surface bias sits at retrieval, not in storage.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=27: 14 in Group 1, 13 in Group 2): Group 1 chose LS over SS 82% of the time (16.46 of 20), chi2=61 (df=12), p<.0001. Group 2 chose AN over FOR only 55% (11 of 20), at chance.
limits: The AN-vs-FOR choice may be insensitive because the FOR cue also shares first-order relations; the authors argue the logic is still that relational info was available. One week delay only.
agent_relevance: Failures to find an analogue should be debugged as a cue problem first. If the stored item contains the structure, a better cue (a structure-explicit rewrite of the current problem) can reach it.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Evidence the paper cites from problem-solving work (restated, not re-run): Gick & Holyoak radiation numbers; Ross (1984, 1989) showed that story-line similarity strongly changes the probability of ACCESSING a prior problem but not the probability of CORRECTLY APPLYING the principle once accessed; Holyoak & Koh, Novick, Reed et al. found surface-driven remindings.
numbers: As reported: Ross 1984, six probability principles taught in different story lines; surface similarity to an appropriate principle helped, to an inappropriate principle hurt, relative to unrelated baseline. (Exact cell values not given in the 1993 text.)
limits: Secondhand: Ross 1984/1989, Holyoak & Koh 1987, Novick 1988 were not opened in this session. Treat as pointers for the follow-up list.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity can also mislead: an irrelevant surface-near case can pull the wrong method. Guardrail: a retrieved case is a hypothesis; G3 (check on held-out evidence) still decides.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: The paper proposes six criteria a retrieval model must meet: structured representations; structural mapping; rare insights (occasional purely relational remindings); primacy of the mundane (most retrievals are literal-similarity matches); surface superiority; scalability. Case-based reasoning with clever indices fails the surface-superiority criterion; plain feature-vector dot products fail the structure criteria. MAC/FAC is built to meet all six.
numbers: Simulation on 9 of the 20 story sets (45 stories). MAC/FAC retrieval ordering LS > SS > AN > FOR matches humans. In a variant with 9 base stories plus 9 FOR distractors, probes LS, SS, AN retrieved the base with proportion 1.0, .89, .67.
limits: Model memory (18 to 36 stories) is far smaller than participants' (32 studied plus lifetime memory), and there is no study-test delay; the authors say only the ORDER of difficulty is at stake.
agent_relevance: The six criteria are a usable checklist for evaluating our own retrieval step: it should mostly return literal matches, sometimes a structural match, run cheaply on a large store.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: MAC/FAC ('many are called but few are chosen') is a two-stage retrieval model. Stage 1 (MAC): for each stored item compute the dot product of content vectors (counts of each predicate/functor in the structured description) with the probe's vector; keep the best item and all within 10% of it. Stage 2 (FAC): run the structure-mapping engine (SME) in literal-similarity mode between probe and each survivor in parallel; keep the best structural score and all within 10%. MAC is cheap and surface-sensitive; FAC is structural.
numbers: Both selectors set to 10%. Dot product of content vectors is an overestimate of the number of match hypotheses SME would build, so it is a good cheap filter. Authors say MAC could run in parallel over very large memories (e.g. connectionist nearest vector).
limits: Memory items are hand-encoded predicate-calculus descriptions. Content vectors count predicate names, so they need canonical (identical) predicate vocabularies; re-representation is assumed to be a separate process. Vocabulary of only a few hundred predicates was tested.
agent_relevance: A direct template for the subgoal library: MAC = fast vector/keyword score over stored subgoals; FAC = code-run structural alignment of probe and candidate (relation graph or typed signature). The program (not the model) does both, in line with section 1 of SCHEMA.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: Fit to human data (Karla the Hawk): MAC/FAC retrieval counts reproduce the human order. In the harder test (all four variants of each base story in memory, 36 stories, base story as probe), literal-similarity and surface matches were retrieved far more than analogies, and FAC rejected most junk.
numbers: Table 4 (probe = base story, memory 36 stories), mean items per probe, MAC output / after FAC: literal LS .78 / .78; surface SF .78 / .44; analogy AN .33 / .22; first-order FOR .22 / 0; other story sets 1.33 / .22. Overall mean items out of MAC 3.4, accepted by FAC 1.6. Easier test (memory 9 base + 9 FOR distractors): base found for LS probes 1.0, SF .89, AN .67. Human recall (Exp 2): LS .56, SF .53, AN .12, FOR .09.
limits: Table 4 cells were read from extracted text where the grid is flattened, and the column pairing was inferred from the means (3.4 and 1.6), so treat decimals as approximate; the companion Law et al. paper prints slightly different cells (SS .67 / .44, AN .33 / .11). The ordinal pattern LS > SF > AN > FOR is stated in the text. MAC/FAC retrieves MORE analogies than people do (the model's task is easier: small memory, no delay).
agent_relevance: A reminder that a two-stage filter returns analogies only when no better surface match competes. If our store has literal matches, they will win; that is fine for reuse, bad for novelty. G8-type tasks need the surface bias switched off on purpose (see operators below).

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: Sensitivity analyses show the fit depends on the theory and is not a parameter accident. With selectors too narrow (MAC 1% or FAC 1%) no analogies get retrieved; too wide gives too many analogies and then junk. Normalisation details do not matter. Using attribute-only or relations-only content vectors changes the result (the all-predicates vector is what fits).
numbers: Original content vectors: viable region MAC and FAC widths of about 10% to 20%; for binary content vectors, viable MAC width about 30% to 50%. Average items out of MAC: 1.5 (standard vectors), 2 (binary).
limits: Only the story data of one lab were simulated. Selector widths are 'weakly constrained by theory'.
agent_relevance: The two knobs (how many MAC survivors, how strict FAC is) are the exact levers for our retrieval budget; G7 says tune them at equal tokens against plain-model baseline, not by taste.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: Section 7.1.7 lists when relational access is NOT poor: (a) experts, who have richer, more uniform relational vocabularies (Novick 1988: experts more often retrieve a structurally similar prior maths problem and reject surface-similar ones faster; Faries & Reiser 1988: after intensive LISP training, subjects accessed structurally similar problems despite surface competitors) and (b) intensive encoding at study (Gick & Holyoak 1983; Catrambone & Holyoak 1987, 1989: comparing two prior analogs raised relational retrieval but merely reading them did not; Schumacher & Gentner 1987: writing out the meaning of proverbs raised relational retrieval; Seifert et al. 1986: priming for thematically similar stories only after judging thematic similarity).
numbers: No new numbers; a review of the cited studies.
limits: These studies were not opened individually. 'Intensive encoding' is vague; the later analogical-encoding work (a19 to a24) gives the operational version.
agent_relevance: Two ways to make relational access good: have the right relational vocabulary (canonical, shared encoding) and process stored items deeply (compare, restate, explain) when storing them. Both can be done at write time in the library.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: Open problems the authors list for MAC/FAC: no retrieval failure (it always returns something unless FAC rejects all); goals are not special (treated as part of the probe's higher-order structure); content vector size when vocabulary is large; no competition between memory items (Wharton et al. 1991, 1992, 1994 found competition between exemplars raises the effect of structural similarity); no iterative access; possible role of re-representation of the probe.
numbers: No numbers. Authors conjecture that active (deliberate) retrieval may be iterative: use the partial matches to re-weight which parts of the probe matter, then query again.
limits: Conjecture only, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Iterative access is what our agent can do that people mostly do not: reformulate the probe (restate the problem in neutral/abstract terms), query again, compare the retrieved items. This is a candidate operator (restate then re-retrieve) that is cheap and code-checkable.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995; journal header 1994) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: How MAC/FAC answers the competing ARCS model (Thagard et al. 1990): MAC/FAC assumes tiered identicality for semantic similarity (non-identical predicates need re-representation), whereas ARCS uses WordNet-style similarity and gives goals/pragmatics a special input. With 100 Aesop fables as distractors, ARCS gave asymptotic activations LS +.67, FOR -.11, SF -.17, AN -.27, which breaks the human order (SF should be near LS; AN should beat FOR).
numbers: ARCS probe results (Karla in memory + 100 fables): LS .67, FOR -.11, SF -.17, AN -.27.
limits: Comparison is between the two teams' encodings and one dataset; the ARCS authors may dispute details. ARCS authors (Holyoak, Thagard) argued that weak semantic similarity is needed or recall would miss too much.
agent_relevance: Two philosophies for the agent: strict canonical vocabulary plus structural check (MAC/FAC) versus soft semantic similarity (embeddings, ARCS). With LLMs, embeddings are the soft option; see a25 to a28 for the LLM evidence.

source: Law, Forbus & Gentner (1994) Simulating similarity-based retrieval: a comparison of ARCS and MAC/FAC
finding: Independent simulation comparison of MAC/FAC and ARCS on the same encodings. MAC/FAC gets the same results as reported for ARCS on the Sour Grapes fable, is about two orders of magnitude faster, is stable when memory grows by 25%, and matches the human ordering on Hawk stories. ARCS is distracted by added plays and may prefer larger descriptions.
numbers: Memory: 100 Aesop fables (+25 Shakespeare plays in Exp 2). Experiment 1: both retrieve Sour Grapes for variant probes; ARCS (0.28), MAC/FAC similar; MAC/FAC runtime about 0.2 to 0.4 s versus 81 to 123 s for ARCS in Exp 1 and 251 to 373 s in Exp 2 (about two orders of magnitude). Exp 2: MAC/FAC unchanged with plays added; ARCS gave 'The Taming of the Shrew' (.22) and 10 other stories for the appearance probe instead of Sour Grapes. Exp 3: probe West Side Story retrieved only Romeo and Juliet in MAC/FAC (FAC score 16.51); probe Hamlet retrieved Romeo and Juliet (6.79), next Julius Caesar 5.49, a drop of about 19%, over the 10% cutoff. Exp 4: ARCS order literal, first-order, appearance, analogy vs human literal, appearance, analogy, first-order; MAC/FAC matched human ordinal order.
limits: The authors could not get ARCS to run on their own encodings (network did not settle after 1,000 iterations, run times up to nine hours), so tests used Thagard's encodings. Authors are the MAC/FAC team (not neutral). ARCS has no formal criterion for what counts as 'retrieved'. Small conference paper, 4 experiments.
agent_relevance: Compute cost matters: a cheap first stage plus a few expensive checks beats a global constraint network. This favours our code-selects design (G5) over a model-judged retrieval.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (Current Directions in Psychological Science overview; year not printed in the extracted text, about 2005) Relational reasoning in a neurally plausible cognitive architecture: an overview of the LISA project
finding: LISA (Learning and Inference with Schemas and Analogies) treats retrieval as 'guided pattern recognition': the target problem is the driver; up to three propositions at a time fire as patterns over shared semantic units (with synchrony binding roles to fillers); these activate stored propositions in long-term memory; retrieval and mapping use the same algorithm, mapping adding learned links. Retrieval is therefore sensitive to semantic (feature) overlap of the roles and fillers, with working memory limited to about three propositions.
numbers: Capacity: at most 3 propositions in working memory at once. The paper says LISA 'provides an excellent fit to the data on analogical reminding in people' (Hummel & Holyoak 1997). War analogy test: about 100 propositions per analog; LISA's preferred mappings matched those most frequently given by people.
limits: Only a 5-page overview (Current Directions) was opened, not the 1997 Psychological Review paper with the access simulations, so exact retrieval numbers (e.g. its replication of Gentner et al. orderings) are not recorded here. The 1997 PDF host refused the connection.
agent_relevance: A second model family: retrieval from role-filler semantic overlap, no separate structural stage. Predicts the same surface bias through shared semantic units. For our agent it is a reminder that a relation-and-role aware index (not whole-text vector) can capture some structure, at the price of capacity limits.

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life: analogical training more powerful than individual case training
finding: Transfer from case training to a real negotiation is almost three times better when people COMPARE two cases and write the shared principle than when they read the same two cases and advise each protagonist. No one in the advice condition noticed the link between the two cases even though they were printed on the same page.
numbers: Masters of Management students, 22 dyads per condition (N=44 dyads): contingency contract used by 14/22 (64%) comparison vs 5/22 (23%) advice, chi2(1, N=44)=7.503, p<.01. Money: dyads with a contingency contract grossed more than dyads that compromised (t(42)=2.484, p<.05; dollar figures garbled in the extracted text); the comparison-over-advice gain in money was a non-significant trend. Quality of principles written in the comparison condition predicted successful transfer; quality of advice in advice condition did not.
quote: not a single person in the Advice condition drew a parallel between the two cases, even though they were presented on the same page.
limits: One negotiation scenario (contingent contracts, 'betting on differences'); well-motivated adult students; transfer to a face-to-face task in the same session, not a delayed one.
agent_relevance: Strongest applied evidence for 'comparison at encoding time'. For us: when the agent solves two similar tasks, run a compare-and-abstract step across the two and store the abstract rule; storing each separately gives close to nothing. Cost is one short extra pass.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams: comparing cases promotes learning and transfer
finding: Replication and extension with negotiation TEAMS. Teams that compared two cases transferred more than teams that analysed them separately; separate analysis was no better than no training at all.
numbers: Contingent contract in the face-to-face negotiation: comparison teams 24/60 = 40% vs separate-case teams 8/37 = 22%, chi2(1, N=97)=3.50, p=.06 (marginal). Comparison vs baseline (no training, individuals): chi2(1, N=83)=4.95, p<.05; separate vs baseline: chi2(1, N=60)<1, ns. Joint gains: comparison M=US$4.76M (SD 1.04) vs separate 4.28M (1.17) vs baseline 4.19M (0.89), F(2,133)=4.35, p<.05. Intact teams vs solo 12/38 = 32%, no reliable difference. All comparison participants described links between the two cases; only 18% of separate-case participants did.
limits: Headline contrast (40% vs 22%) is only marginally significant; effect smaller than in a19. Same authors, same scenario family.
agent_relevance: Gives a smaller, more realistic effect size (40% vs 22%) to plan around. Separate study of cases being no better than no training is a warning for any 'few-shot examples' design: examples sitting next to each other in context do not produce an abstraction unless the comparison is requested.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events
finding: Late analogical abstraction (comparing two analogous examples at RECALL time, not study time) improves retrieval of relationally similar cases from people's own memory. This is the key access finding: comparison builds an abstract schema, and the schema is a better probe than either example alone.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=124 management consultants; 64 comparison, 60 separate-case): retrieved good contingent-contract examples M=1.25 (comparison) vs 0.82 (separate), t(122)=2.65, p<.01. Types of retrieval (comparison / separate): analogy 63% / 42%; shallow match 20% / 40%; literal 8% / 5%; no reminding 9% / 13%. Overall 52% analogy, 30% shallow, 6% literal, 11% none (110 recalled items). Exp 2 (N=36 Masters of Accounting): same direction. Exp 3 (contingent contracts and trade-offs; comparison M=1.08 vs control M=0.50 on a 0 to 2 scale; F(1,48)=10.38, p<.005).
quote: Schema abstraction from analogical examples can revive otherwise inert knowledge.
limits: Retrieval was from real-life memory, coded by judges; there is a chance of confabulation (answered by Exp 4 with a fixed memory set). Sample are working professionals in a negotiation training setting.
agent_relevance: This is the paper to build the retrieval design on: compare two current analogous problems, abstract the shared relational schema, use that schema as the retrieval probe against the library. It gives the agent a way to turn a surface-biased index into a structure-biased one at the price of one extra pass.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events
finding: Exp 4 and 5 control the memory set. Comparison of two probe examples at test time raised recall of the earlier analogous example and CUT retrieval of the surface-similar one. Exp 5 reproduces the Gick and Holyoak tumour problem with a delay and gets a much higher solve rate with comparison.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=73): recalled the prior analogous example 27% (comparison) vs 6% (separate), chi2(1, N=73)=6.12, p<.05 (about 4x). Surface-similar retrieval: 30% vs 78% (same chi2 reported in the text). Exp 5 (N=227, filled delay after the initial story): tumour problem solved 31% (comparison) vs 5% (separate), chi2(1, N=227)=24.71, p<.001; Red Adair (oil-well fire) problem 41% vs 30%, chi2=2.89, p=.08, ns. Kurtz & Loewenstein (2007), cited there: comparing two test problems gave about 50% on the tumour problem.
limits: The separate-case group did well on the fire-hose problem (30%), maybe because physical hose knowledge is common; not a clean replication of the radiation result. Surface retrieval drop (78% to 30%) shows comparison shifts WHAT is retrieved, not only how many.
agent_relevance: Shows a mechanism that works on an unchanged memory store: change the probe. For the agent, a probe built from two instances of the current problem class (or the current problem plus one solved instance) should pull structural neighbours and push away surface-near wrong ones.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events
finding: Simulation with MAC/FAC on the Karla the Hawk set (7 story sets) shows the same pattern: relational schemas built by SME's abstraction as probes retrieve analogical matches, whereas single-story probes retrieve literal and shallow matches. Relational schemas stored in memory are also themselves easier to retrieve than single analogs.
numbers: Simulation 1: single story probes retrieved shallow matches 86% (Story 1) / 100% (Story 2) and analogical matches 14% / 0%; relational schema probes retrieved analogical matches 86%, shallow 29%, first-order matches 14%. Schemas had about 80% relational predicates vs about 40% in individual stories. Simulation 3: a base probe retrieved 57% of stored relational schemas but only 14% of the analogical matches; with literal matches added (Sim 4) literal matches dominated (100%).
limits: Seven story sets, hand-encoded; the 'schemas' are SME-generated generalisations.
agent_relevance: The retrieval filter can be computed: abstract the shared structure of two cases in code (keep the relations, drop the object names) and use that as the MAC probe. This is code, not a model judgment, so it fits G5.

source: Kurtz, Miao & Gentner (2001) Learning by analogical bootstrapping
finding: Mutual alignment ('analogical bootstrapping'): comparing two partly understood analogous scenarios promotes understanding of the shared causal structure, but only when the comparison is intensive (jointly interpreting the scenarios AND listing correspondences). Casual presentation of the two is no better than one.
numbers: Exp 1 (heat flow scenarios, N=80; 4 conditions: control, separated, joint, joint+correspondence): causal relevance of listed differences differed by condition F(3,76)=2.75, p<.05, only joint+correspondence beat control (Dunnett p<.05). 48% of participants in the joint-interpretation conditions used all three key terms (heat, transfer, cause) vs 23% in the non-comparing conditions. Exp 2: correspondence-only did worse than joint+correspondence on correct answers, t(9)=2.684, p<.05.
limits: Concerned with encoding and abstraction, not with retrieval itself. Differences between conditions on the description task were not significant (F(3,76)=2.09, p=.10). Small cells.
agent_relevance: Gives an operational definition of 'intensive comparison': a joint description plus an explicit list of which element maps to which. A prompt that only says 'here are two examples' is the weak version. Make the alignment explicit and checkable (listed pairs).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Analogical prompting asks the model, in a single pass, to first recall (self-generate) K relevant example problems with solutions, optionally also a piece of knowledge/tutorial, then solve the new problem. Idea: the model has seen related problems in training; naming them in context acts as a self-made retrieval.
numbers: Prompt asks for 'relevant exemplars' then 'solve the initial problem'. K=5 for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench; for Codeforces both knowledge and K=3 exemplars. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2, text-davinci-001/002/003, text-curie-001.
quote: outperforms 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT across a range of tasks and base LLMs, achieving an average accuracy gain of +4%.
limits: One pass; no code check of exemplar quality. Authors' headline is an average gain of +4% over 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT.
agent_relevance: This is retrieval by generation rather than by index: the model plays both the memory and the retriever. Under G4 it is not independent evidence; the generated 'similar problems' share the model's blind spots.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Measured gains are small on easy maths tasks and larger on harder or structured ones. On GSM8K and MATH the self-generated exemplars add about 1 to 3 points over fixed hand-written few-shot CoT with GPT-3.5 and PaLM2; on GPT-3.5 BIG-Bench tasks gains are several points over 0-shot CoT; Codeforces gains need generated knowledge.
numbers: GSM8K (0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 5-shot CoT / ours): GPT-3.5-turbo 75.0 / 75.8 / 76.7 / 77.8; text-davinci-003 14.8 / 50.3 / 54.0 / 61.0; PaLM2 60.8 / 78.2 / 80.7 / 81.7. MATH: GPT-3.5 33.0 / 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3; PaLM2 27.1 / 29.8 / 34.3 / 34.8. BIG-Bench (GPT-3.5, 0-shot / CoT / 3-shot / ours): word sorting 66.8 / 67.6 / 68.4 / 75.2; logical deduction 30.0 / 35.2 / 36.4 / 41.6; temporal sequences 40.4 / 44.8 / 58.0 / 57.6 (3-shot wins); colored objects 50.4 / 61.6 / 62.0 / 68.0; formal fallacies 53.6 / 55.6 / 55.6 / 58.8. Codeforces Acc@1 / Acc@10: GPT-3.5-16k 8/24 (0-shot), 9/27 (CoT), 11/27 (3-shot), 13/25 (ours exemplars), 15/29 (knowledge + exemplars); GPT-4 16/30, 16/29, 17/31, 17/32, 19/37.
limits: Single runs, no confidence intervals or seeds are given in the table. Gain on GSM8K with GPT-3.5 (77.8 vs 76.7) is about one point and may be inside noise for GSM8K sample size. Table column mapping read from extracted text.
agent_relevance: Measured gain is modest and model-dependent. A self-generated analogue is a cheap prompt; it should be tested at equal tokens against plain CoT and best-of-N before it earns a place (G7).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-generation beats retrieval from a labelled training set only when the base model is strong. With weak models, retrieving real labelled exemplars is better. This is the measured trade-off between index retrieval and self-generated 'memory'.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy by model (0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 5-shot fixed / 5-shot retrieved / ours): text-curie-001 2 / 2 / 2 / 3 / 2; text-davinci-001 6 / 6 / 10 / 11 / 9; text-davinci-002 13 / 22 / 43 / 47 / 48; text-davinci-003 14 / 50 / 54 / 57 / 61. Number of exemplars K on GSM8K / MATH (GPT-3.5): K=1 76.1 / 34.8; K=2 77.0 / 36.7; K=3 77.5 / 37.3; K=4 77.3 / 37.0; K=5 77.8 / 37.1.
limits: Retrieval used the GSM8K train set (labelled, similar domain), an easy setting for retrieval; real library retrieval would be on noisier stores. Retrieved exemplars were chosen by embedding similarity (surface); no structure-based retrieval baseline was run.
agent_relevance: For a small/weak base model our agent should lean on an external verified library, not on self-generation; for strong models either works but the library has the advantage of being checked. Using K=3 or more is safer than one exemplar (K=1 'relies too much on a single exemplar').

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Failure analysis of 100 problems (50 solved, 50 unsolved from GSM8K and MATH): most failures happen even though the generated exemplars are relevant and correct, because of a generalisation gap (new problem harder than the exemplar), over-reliance on a specific exemplar, or other slips. Few failures are due to irrelevant exemplars.
numbers: Of 50 correct: 35 exemplars relevant and correct, 9 relevant but with wrong solution, 6 irrelevant. Of 50 incorrect: 28 relevant and correct but model still failed (12 generalisation gap, 8 over-reliance on a specific exemplar, 8 other, e.g. calculation); 12 relevant but incorrect; 10 irrelevant. So 9 of 50 correct answers came from WRONG exemplars (relevance is not the whole story).
limits: Manual labelling by the authors; small sample (100).
agent_relevance: Two things to avoid in the agent: copying a retrieved case's wrong detail (over-reliance), and treating a similar-but-easier case as sufficient. The G3 check on held-out inputs catches both. Also: correct answers with wrong exemplars show the gain may partly be a format/reasoning-priming effect, not retrieval.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer (Memory & Cognition 15, 332-340)
finding: Source analog (lightbulb filament story) and target (radiation problem) with surface and structural similarity varied. Both kinds of similarity aid spontaneous retrieval; spontaneous transfer can survive a delay of days if source and target share at least one salient surface feature; accuracy of use depends on structural (causal) match.

source: Wharton, Holyoak, Downing, Lange, Wickens & Melz (1994) Below the surface: analogical similarity and retrieval competition in reminding (Cognitive Psychology 26, 64-101)
finding: Retrieval competition: when two semantically related passages compete in memory, retrieval is impaired overall, but a structurally consistent (analogical) cue gains an edge; analogical similarity shows an effect on reminding mainly in the competition condition. Offered as the main evidence that structure can matter at access.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving (Cognitive Psychology 12, 306-355)
finding: The founding experiments: Duncker radiation problem with the fortress story. Reported figures from secondary summaries: about 10% solve without an analog, about 30% after reading the analogous story without a hint, about 75% once told to use the story. Control stories (irrelevant analog) did not help.
